growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings are pea-sized green globes with tiny spines, nearly always under a nurse shrub or tree. They elongate into a single thick, ribbed, grey-green column, much spinier than adults (old cardons can be almost spineless); after decades arms branch from low on the trunk and turn upward like a candelabra.
growth.source: Radiocarbon dating of cardon spines (Radiocarbon journal): growth 3-23 cm/yr, mean 9.8 cm/yr, faster in taller plants; Wikipedia (slow-growing, lifespan hundreds of years, tallest 19.2 m); El cardon gigante (Acta Universitaria 2017); age at first flowering estimated

fruiting.source: USA-NPN photo guide (milky-white flowers late spring; fruit turns reddish and splits to show red pulp; lesser long-nosed bats depend on its nectar); Nativas Landscape (flowers open late afternoon, die next day around noon); Acta Universitaria (flowering-fruiting Apr-Sep); fruit size, set and crop estimated

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling: a tiny fan of thick, triangular, blue-green leaves in two ranks, often pale-spotted and edged with small teeth, later twisting into a spiral rosette. For years it stays a squat rosette; then a single stout trunk lifts it and at 1-2 m the crown forks again and again into a rounded head of rosettes. Old bark peels in golden, sharp-edged plates.
growth.source: Wikipedia (slow growth, stems repeatedly fork in two) and SANBI PlantZAfrica as recalled (tree aloe to 7-9 m of Namibia and the Northern Cape; first flowers at about 20-30 yr; large trees thought well over a century old). Two-ranked spotted seedling leaves as in most aloes; rates estimated.

fruiting.source: German Wikipedia (Koecherbaum: 3-5-branched inflorescence to 30 cm with cylindrical racemes to 15 cm; bulbous flowers 33 mm long, bright canary-yellow; nectar favoured by sunbirds). Winter (Jun-Jul) flowering, bee visits, capsules with papery winged seeds, timings and crop estimated from SANBI as recalled and related tree aloes.

growth.juvenile_note: Two tiny fleshy cotyledons, then a pea-sized spiny green ball only ~6 mm tall at 2 years and 13-19 mm wide at 8 months in a nursery. It survives only in the shade of a nurse plant (palo verde, ironwood, bursage), stays a small ribbed spiny knob or short column for decades (1 m at 20-50 yr), and grows its first arms at 75-100 years.
growth.source: NRCS Tucson PMC saguaro propagation (60 days ~3 mm; 4-5 yr to 15 cm; to 200 yr); Wikipedia Saguaro (1 m at 20-50 yr; ~41 yr at 3 m, 83 yr at 6 m, 157 yr at 10.7 m; arms at 75-100 yr; nurse plants); first flowers at ~2.2 m (35-70 yr) per Steenbergh & Lowe

fruiting.source: Arizona-Sonora Desert Museum fact sheet (white flowers ~8 cm, open at night <24 h; lesser long-nosed and Mexican long-tongued bats, bees, white-winged doves; red fruit with up to 2000 seeds); NRCS (bloom late Apr-early Jun, fruit ripe ~37 days after flowering); Wikipedia (~4 flowers/day for a month, fruits 6-9 cm, split open)

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: two oval cotyledons, then tiny feathery bipinnate leaves on a thin stem with paired spines, some long, straight and white, others short and hooked. The taproot dives deep first. Browsed saplings become dense, low, cage-like spiny bushes for years; once a leader escapes browsers it gains about 1.5 m in two years and only later spreads the flat umbrella crown.
growth.source: ICRAF Agroforestree (Acacia tortilis): up to 21 m, about 1.5 m in 2 years, a 6-7-year-old tree yields 5-6 kg of clean seed, 10-12 kg pods a year at 10 yr; Andersen & Krzywinski 2007 (BMC Ecology): radiocarbon ages of 200-650 yr for trees in Egypt's Eastern Desert, radial growth up to 2.4 mm a year. Germination and height curve estimated.

fruiting.source: ICRAF Agroforestree (Acacia tortilis): white or pale yellowish-white heads 0.5-1.1 cm, pods 7-10 cm by 6-10 mm, spirally twisted, 10-12 kg pods per 10-yr tree; the Turkana make porridge from the pods, the Maasai eat immature seeds; Wikipedia: aromatic flowers, springlike coiled pods. Flowering at the onset of the rains, ripening, pod fall and rot times estimated.

On dry uplands it grows only a few cm a year (about 5 cm at 9 months, 11 cm at 38 months) while the taproot plunges 50-85 cm; along washes and floodplains it becomes a single-trunked tree with a broad, spreading umbrella crown.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Prosopis velutina (over 80% germination at 16-38 C; seed in pods germinates over 1-3 yr in soil; upland seedlings 5.3 cm at 9 months, 11.4 cm at 38 months, roots 51-85 cm; nursery 17 cm in 12 months). Height to maturity, age at first fruit and lifespan estimated from mesquite literature.

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS P. velutina (yellowish-green flowers on 5-7.6 cm spikelike racemes, pollinated mainly by bees; pods 7.6-20 cm mature about 7-9 weeks after bud burst, ripe in July and drop in September, some June-Oct). Flowers per raceme, crop, fruit set, colours and decay estimated.

Young plants are twiggy, yellow-green-barked shrubs whose stiff side twigs end in thorns; leaves appear only after rain and soon drop, so the green bark does most of the photosynthesis.
growth.source: Wikipedia (slow-growing, sometimes living several hundred years; seedlings drought-sensitive for 2-3 months, ~1.6% survive; rodents cache and plant the seeds); growth to size and first flowering estimated from long-term Sonoran Desert plot records of slow foothill paloverde growth

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (small pale-yellow flowers at branch ends in late spring, not every year; soft 4-8 cm pods constricted between the seeds ripen in July and stick to the branches); bee pollination and green seeds eaten by Sonoran peoples from regional ethnobotany; set and crop estimated

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: a tiny green knob with two fleshy cotyledons, soon covered in fine white spines; stays a small spiny globe for years (often in the shade of a nurse shrub), growing a few cm a year and gaining its hooked reddish central spines. At 20-30 cm across it starts to flower; it lengthens into a ribbed barrel and, when tall, leans toward the south-southwest.
growth.source: USDA FEIS (Ferocactus wislizeni: germination best at 20-30 C with >=8 h light; lifespan 50-130 yr); Wikipedia (0.9-1.8 m, rarely 3 m; 50-100 yr). Growth rate and first flowering estimated from barrel-cactus growth.

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS (flowers sporadically in late spring, profusely Jul-Sep; fruit yellow, barrel-shaped, fleshy); Wikipedia (yellow to red-orange flowers visited by cactus bees Lithurgus; fruits persist atop the plant, sometimes >1 yr; eaten by deer, javelina, ground squirrels; sour but edible). Flower size, counts, ripening estimated.

The young plant is a thin, sparse, zig-zag-stemmed sprig; it branches from the base into an open, vase-shaped bush of grey stems, and after decades the centre dies so the clone spreads outward as a ring.
growth.source: USDA WPSM (Larrea: flowers mainly spring, some all year; white-villous capsule splitting into 5 one-seeded carpels, ripe late spring-early summer; fruits sparingly at 4-6 yr, fully at 8-13 yr; establishment rare); Wikipedia (1-3 m; crowns split at 30-90 yr; King Clone ring ~11,700 yr). Growth rate estimated.

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (flowers to 25 mm, five yellow twisted petals, visited by 22 bee species; fuzzy spherical capsule splitting into five one-seeded carpels); USDA WPSM (densely white-villous fruit maturing late spring-early summer). Flower life, set, crop and rot estimated.
